questions.stem: A 27-year-old pregnant woman spent the day with her nephew at a family celebration. The following day he developed a widespread vesicular rash which was diagnosed as chickenpox (primary varicella-zoster virus infection). She contacted her obstetrician the same day concerned about the risks of chickenpox as she had never had this illness and had not been vaccinated. She was 34 weeks pregnant and had mild asthma.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Send serum for VZV IgG testing

questions.explanation: Send serum for VZV IgG testing The patient’s history suggests that she may be naïve to VZV infection, and therefore although she is in the 3rd trimester and the fetus is not at risk of congenital varicella syndrome, she is at risk of severe varicella disease if infection occurs. There is also a risk that delivery may occur around the time of clinical illness if she is infected, risking perinatal transmission to the neonate. As she has sought medical attention promptly following exposure, it is appropriate to assess her preexisting immunity by checking her VZV IgG status before ordering the administration of VZIG, which is effective if given within 10 days of exposure. Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine and therefore is not appropriate in pregnancy. Aciclovir/valaciclovir prophylaxis is also not recommended to avert clinical illness in pregnant women exposed to chickenpox.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q19

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 48-hour history of rash. He had a background of polymyalgia rheumatica and was taking prednisolone 40 mg OD. The lesions first appeared over the left side of his face but had spread over the past 24 hours. On examination his temperature was 38.5°C. There were vesicular lesions over his face, torso, and limbs.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation: VZV PCR of lesion This patient is relatively immunocompromised on long-term steroids. The distribution of rash suggests the possibility of herpes zoster, or shingles. Subsequent widespread development of vesicular lesions indicates the possibility of disseminated zoster. In the presence of clinical uncertainly, the most definitive investigation would be PCR of vesicular fluid to confirm virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q26

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman sought medical advice 48 hours after a significant chickenpox exposure. She was 32 weeks pregnant with no personal history of chickenpox. She had not received the varicella vaccine. Investigations: Varicella IgG negative. She was treated with VZV immunoglobulin (VZIG).
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate definition of her treatment?
questions.explanation: Passive immunization This is an example of passive immunization, that is, the induction of immunity by transfer of antibodies to the nonimmune host. Vaccine immunization describes a method of immunization; partial immunization occurs when a person becomes ill with an infection but is not susceptible to severe illness or death; natural immunization is induction of immunity in a host who is exposed to the live pathogen; active immunization is the induction of immunity by antigen exposure, usually by vaccination.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q45

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was reviewed 24 hours after a significant chickenpox exposure. She had acute myeloid leukemia and was undergoing treatment. She had been treated with human varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) 9 weeks previously after her varicellazoster virus (VZV) IgG was found to be negative after another significant chickenpox exposure.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Recheck VZV IgG This is to assess her immune status and re-administer VZIG as soon as possible if found to be varicella susceptible. Where possible, immune status should be tested in immune compromised individuals prior to the administration of VZIG. VZIG offers no additional protection to individuals who have VZV antibody. Patients may still develop chickenpox, however, following administration of VZIG, and therefore advice to commence antivirals should lesions develop is essential. A proportion of patients will seroconvert in the absence of clinical disease. For this reason, repeat testing for immune status is indicated, as in this case. If an exposure occurs after 3 weeks a further dose of VZIG is required if the individual is still varicella susceptible.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q13

questions.stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman attended her GP at 14/40 as her 2-year-old daughter had developed a rash and fever consistent with chickenpox that morning. She had been born and brought up in the UK. She was unsure of her varicella immune status.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ask her to re-attend if a rash illness develops
Give her intramuscular varicella zoster immunoglobulin
Reassure her that she is likely to be immune

questions.explanation: Check her varicella-zoster IgG She may require VZIG to reduce the risk of severe maternal disease and to reduce the risk of fetal varicella syndrome, but as it is a human product and there is time, she should have her immunity checked first, as she may be immune already.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q45

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man sought medical help after learning that he had had a significant exposure to chickenpox 24 hours earlier. He had no personal history of chickenpox and had not received the varicella vaccine. He had a history of hypertension and diabetes, and was taking enalapril and metformin. He had no known drug allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Administer varicella vaccine The chickenpox (varicella) vaccine would be recommended for all healthy adults who are exposed to chickenpox and do not know their immune status. Reasons for this are twofold. There is some evidence that vaccine may be effective in preventing chickenpox if given within 3 days of exposure. It is also an opportunity to protect the patient against future varicella exposures if they do not contract chickenpox on this occasion, so should be given irrespective of the interval since exposure. Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG/VZIG) is recommended for susceptible pregnant women and immunosuppressed individuals who have had a significant exposure. Intravenous immune globulin is not recommended. Valaciclovir is not indicated as prophylaxis for healthy adults but could be used to protect immunosuppressed individuals. Measuring titers may not provide an answer in time to give the vaccine and is not considered cost effective.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q28

questions.question: Zostavax

parts.text: A.  What is the efficacy in preventing zoster?
B.  At what age is it recommended?
C.  Contraindicated in or not for following: I. Unknown serostatus or history of vzv. Ii. Steroids. IIi. Hairy cell leukemia. Iv. CGD? V. COPD on intermittent steroids.

cohort_answer.text:
Zostavax (live) – 51% reduction in risk of zoster, 67% reduction of PHN; Shingrix (recombinant, inactivated) - 91% at preventing shingles and 97% PHN
Zostavax 60 or older 1 dose SC; Shingrix 50 or older 2 doses IM
Unknown serostatus: Yes because no need to check status before giving but, needs varicella vaccine if not immune/didn't have natural disease; Steroids: Yes if on high dose and for longer than 14 days (delay 1month after d/c); Hairy cell leukemia: Yes; CGD: No (cannot give live bacterial vaccines to CGD); Copd on intermittent steroids: No. Stop antivirals 24 hours prior to giving vaccine. Wait 1 year after an episode of shingles before giving either vaccine (or receiving Zostavax, wait a year to get Shingrix). Shingrix not approved in immunocompromised population yet. Can give in pregnancy.

questions.question: A woman enquires about varicella vaccination.

parts.text: What are 3 contraindications?

cohort_answer.text: Pregnancy; Immunocompromised/suppressed; Active untreated TB; History of anaphylaxis after previous administration of the product and in persons with proven immediate or anaphylactic hypersensitivity to any component of the product, with the exception of egg allergy for MMRV vaccine; Primary immunodeficiency; Anti-viral within past 48hrs; IVIg within past 8mos/VarZig within past 5 mos; Chronic ASA therapy.

questions.question: Rash on arms of a 10yo child. Vesicular lesions. [image-based question: EM shown is of herpesviridae]

parts.text: What 2 organisms would be consistent with this?

questions.model_answer: Two organisms consistent with vesicular rash and herpesvirus-family EM findings: herpes simplex virus (HSV-1/HSV-2) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

questions.question: 19. A 65 year old woman present with zosteriform lesions in a V1 distribution.

parts.text: List 2 clear indications to initiate treatment for zoster (in a general sense, not for this patient)
b) List 4 neurological [complications] of herpes zoster reactivation

c) Her husband (67 years old) is curious about how he could decrease his risk of zoster. What percentage of zoster episodes and what percentage of neurological complication would the zoster vaccine prevent?

cohort_answer.text: Indications: 1. <72hr of clinical symptoms or >72 hours if new lesions still appearing. 2. Complicated/disseminated zoster: Zoster ophthalmicus (V1, trigeminal ganglion) - sight-threatening; Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion, multiple CN) - lesions in external auditory canal/loss of taste anterior 2/3 tongue, ipsilateral facial nerve palsy. 3. Immunocompromised host (even if >72hrs). Goals of antiviral therapy: lessen severity/duration of pain, promote faster healing, prevent new lesions, decrease viral shedding/transmission risk, prevent post herpetic neuralgia. Neurological complications: 1. Post-herpetic neuralgia (10-15%); 2. Herpes Zoster ophthalmicus - conjunctivitis, episcleritis, keratitis (2/3), iritis (40%), Hutchinson's sign; 3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome - triad of ipsilateral facial paralysis, ear pain+vesicles in auditory canal, loss of taste anterior 2/3 tongue; 4. Aseptic meningitis/encephalitis; 5. Transverse myelitis; 6. Peripheral motor neuropathy; 7. Stroke syndromes; 8. Bells palsy.

questions.question: Zostavax vaccination

parts.text: What is the effectiveness of preventing shingles?
What is the recommended age?
Is the vaccine contraindicated: Breast Ca with adjuvant chemo stopped 6 months ago?
Is the vaccine contraindicated: Prednisone 40mg/day
Is the vaccine contraindicated: Prednisone short course and inhaled corticosteroids for asthma
Is the vaccine contraindicated: CGD
Is the vaccine contraindicated: Hairy Cell Leukemia

cohort_answer.text:
Effectiveness: 51% effective at preventing shingles; 67% effective at preventing post herpetic neuralgia. Shingrix: >90% for both, give to =>50yo
Recommended age: 60 years of age and older. Can be given between 50–59 years of age, as efficacy data exists for this age group but it should be noted that the incidence of Herpes zoster increases with age and is higher after the age of 60, and that the vaccine's protective immunity appears to wane after 5-7 years
Breast Ca with adjuvant chemo stopped 6 months ago: No. PHAC: If immunization cannot be completed prior to initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, generally a period of at least 3 months should elapse between therapy cessation and the administration of inactivated vaccines (if possible, to ensure maximum immunogenicity) or live vaccines (to reduce the risk of disease caused by the vaccine strain).
Prednisone 40mg/day: Yes. Short term corticosteroid therapy is not a contraindication to immunization (i.e., < 14 days); or a low-to-moderate dose of prednisone or equivalent (less than 2 mg/kg/day, or less than 20 mg/day if weight > 10 kg); or long-term, alternate-day treatment with short-acting preparations; or maintenance physiologic replacement therapy; or administered topically, inhaled, or locally injected (e.g., joint injection).
Prednisone short course and inhaled corticosteroids for asthma: No
CGD: No – only live bacterial vaccines are C/I in CGD (bcg/typhoid)
Hairy Cell Leukemia: Yes

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant calls you on April 2. Her son has chicken pox, with a rash starting on March 27. Today, on April 2, his lesions are crusted. She is VZV serology negative.

parts.text: What is your next step in management?
A calendar of March through April is given. Circle the first day and last day on which the pregnant woman could be contagious.
If she develops lesions, what do you give her, if anything?

questions.model_answer:
a) Next step: give VariZIG (varicella-zoster immune globulin) as soon as possible - she is a seronegative pregnant woman with a significant household exposure.
b) Contagious period of the son: from about 2 days before rash onset (~March 25) until all lesions are crusted (crusting noted April 2, so last contagious day is approximately April 1).
c) If she develops lesions (breakthrough varicella despite VariZIG, or infection not prevented): treat with oral valacyclovir/acyclovir, or IV acyclovir if severe or pulmonary symptoms develop, given the risk of severe varicella/pneumonia in pregnancy.

Q34 (2018)
A 60-year old man is interested in the vaccine against zoster. Compare and contrast
Brand Name of Vaccine | Live or Recombinant | Adjuvant Used | Number of Doses | Effectiveness in his age group
SHINGRIX | | | |
ZOSTAVAX II | | | |

parts.text: Compare and contrast SHINGRIX and ZOSTAVAX II: Live or Recombinant, Adjuvant Used, Number of Doses, Effectiveness in his age group

cohort_answer.text:
SHINGRIX | Recombinant | Yes (AS01B) | 2 | >90%
ZOSTAVAX II | Live | None | 1 | 50%
Mechanism of Action of AS01B Adjuvant: AS01B adjuvant induces a local and transient activation of the innate immune system by two immune enhancers: MPL, which signals through Toll-like Receptor 4, and QS-21 signaling which involves activity of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex. These two agonists activate antigen presenting cells loaded with antigen in the draining lymph node that enables recruitment of naive CD4+ T cells. Both MPL and QS-21 are required to induce the maximal frequencies of gE-specific cytokine-producing CD4+ T cells and the highest titers of gE-specific antibodies.

questions.question: 6yo girl with primary varicella.

parts.text: Aside from immuncompromised state, name 3 reasons you’d treat her with acyclovir.
4 reasons to give VZIG

questions.model_answer:
a) Reasons (besides immunocompromise) to treat a healthy child's primary varicella with acyclovir: (1) age older than 12 years (2) chronic cutaneous or pulmonary disorder (e.g., eczema, asthma) (3) long-term salicylate (aspirin) therapy (risk of Reye syndrome) - a secondary household case (often more severe) is another accepted indication.
b) Reasons to give VariZIG: (1) immunocompromised, VZV-susceptible individual with significant exposure (2) susceptible (seronegative) pregnant woman with significant exposure (3) newborn whose mother had varicella onset from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery (4) hospitalized premature infant (≥28 weeks gestation) whose mother lacks evidence of immunity, or any premature infant <28 weeks/<1000 g regardless of maternal history.

questions.question: Regarding Varicella infection:

parts.text: Aside from an immunocompromised state, name THREE indications to treat a 6 year-old boy with primary Varicella infection?
In general, what are FOUR indications to treat with VZIg?

cohort_answer.text: Indications to treat: Encephalitis; Pneumonia; Hepatitis; High risk for SSTI. VZIG indications: Immunocompromised host; Pregnant women who lack evidence of immunity; Newborns of mothers who developed varicella 5 days before and 2 days after delivery; Premature >28wks with no evidence of maternal immunity; ALL premature <28wks or <1kg at birth (regardless of mom's immunity)

questions.question: 5 year old boy who just completed a 1 month therapy of steroids (2mg/kg). Now admitted to hospital. His roommate just diagnosed with varicella.

parts.text: Name 3 ways to prove protection to varicella
Exposed patient has to stay in hospital, what kind of precautions are required for the exposed patient and for what duration.
In the following situation, give when you can vaccinate the patient described in the stem with the varicella vaccine: Parents refuse to give VarZIG
Patient received VarZIG

questions.model_answer:
a) Three ways to prove varicella protection: (1) documented history of physician-diagnosed varicella (2) documented receipt of 2 doses of varicella vaccine (3) positive VZV IgG serology.
b) The exposed, non-immune patient requires airborne plus contact precautions from day 8 through day 21 after exposure (extended to day 28 if VariZIG was administered, due to a prolonged incubation period).
c) If parents refuse VariZIG: the child cannot be given the live varicella vaccine while still significantly immunosuppressed - vaccination should be deferred until at least 1 month (4 weeks) after high-dose corticosteroids have been discontinued.
d) If the patient received VariZIG: live varicella vaccine should be deferred for at least 5 months after VariZIG administration, since the immune globulin can blunt the vaccine immune response.
questions.beyond_mandell: Precise precaution durations and vaccine deferral intervals reflect standard AAP Red Book/CDC guidance.

questions.question: Varicella vs. Herpes Zoster vaccine.

parts.text: Give the one main difference between the Varicella and Live-Attenuated Herpes Zoster vaccine
In the following scenarios would you give the varicella or HZ vaccine: 24yo F, non-pregnant, Varicella IgG negative
51M, history of chickenpox, immune competent
75F, negative varicella IgG, immune competent

What are three comparative advantages of the currently recommended HZ vaccine (did not say to what but presumably testing that you know the recommended vaccine is RZV and asking what the advantages are compared to LAIV)

questions.model_answer:
a) Main difference: the varicella vaccine is a standard-titer live-attenuated (Oka strain) vaccine given to VZV-susceptible individuals to prevent primary infection (chickenpox), whereas the live zoster vaccine (Zostavax) contains a much higher titer of the same Oka strain and is intended to boost pre-existing VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity in previously infected individuals to prevent reactivation (shingles) - they are not interchangeable.
b) 24-year-old F, non-pregnant, varicella IgG negative: give the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine (2-dose series).
c) 51-year-old M, history of chickenpox, immunocompetent: give the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), recommended for immunocompetent adults ≥50 years regardless of prior varicella/zoster history or serostatus.
d) 75-year-old F, negative varicella IgG, immunocompetent: give the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) - ACIP does not recommend serologic testing before zoster vaccination, as most older adults have been infected despite a negative/unreliable history or test.
e) Three comparative advantages of the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) over the live zoster vaccine: (1) substantially higher efficacy (>90% vs. ~50%) (2) efficacy is better maintained in older age groups (≥70 years) and over time, with less waning (3) it is a non-live subunit vaccine, so it can be given to immunocompromised patients in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated.
questions.beyond_mandell: Current ACIP recommendations for Shingrix preference and age criteria.

questions.question: You get a call on April 2nd about a pregnant woman whose son has just had chicken pox. He developed the rash on March 27th. It has now crusted over.

parts.text: What do you do for the pregnant patient?
For how long should she be isolated? Select the start date and the stop date on a calendar.
If the woman develops varicella, how would you treat it?

cohort_answer.text: Varicella Antibodies (if patient does not know history); if negative give VZIg. DON'T vaccinate, it's contraindicated in pregnancy. Indications for VZIg: susceptible patient, significant exposure, increased risk, post exposure immunization contraindicated. Maximal benefit of VZIg is early after exposure; <96 hours ideal, >96 hours <10 days you still do it but more to attenuate the illness. Individuals considered immune to varicella: documented evidence of immunization with 2 doses of a varicella-containing vaccine; laboratory evidence of immunity. In case of hematopoietic stem cell transplant, administer VarIg regardless of VZV IgG result. If serology results cannot be obtained within 96 hours, VarIg should be administered. (PHAC) || Isolation: susceptible patient's exposure to VZV should be in contact and airborne precautions from 8th day after the first contact to 21 days after the last contact (CDC). || Treatment if she develops varicella: UpToDate - oral acyclovir therapy (800 mg five times per day for seven days) for all pregnant women with uncomplicated varicella. Stanford: Acyclovir 800 mg po 5x/day or 10 mg/KG IV q8h x 5 days.

questions.question: A 60-year old man is interested in the vaccination to prevent zoster.

parts.text: Compare and contrast Shingrix and Zostavax: Brand Name, Live or Recombinant, Adjuvant Used, Number of Doses, Effectiveness in his Age Group

cohort_answer.text: Shingrix: recombinant zoster vaccine, glycoprotein E antigen + adjuvant, two doses 2-6 months apart; population >=70: 89% reduction in risk of HZ; population >=50: 96.2% reduction. Zostavax: zoster vaccine live, one dose; population >=60: 51% reduction; population 50-59: 70% reduction

questions.question: VZV

parts.text: In an immunocompetent individual, list 3 reasons to treat.
List 4 reasons to give VZIG (following potential exposure).

cohort_answer.text: Reasons to treat: patients presenting with acute infection ≤72 hours; zoster ophthalmicus (prevent retinal involvement); any neurologic involvement (meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis); chronic cutaneous or pulmonary disorders; those receiving long-term salicylate therapy (prevent Reye's syndrome). VZIG reasons: immunocompromised patients of any age; pregnant females without immunity (up to 10 days after exposure); hospitalized neonates ≥28 weeks whose mothers lack immunity; hospitalized neonates <28 weeks regardless of mother's immunity; neonates whose mothers develop VZV 5 days prior to 2 days after birth.

questions.question: Zostivax.

parts.text: What is efficacy in reducing shingles.
What age should be given at?
Patient starting anti-TNF therapy, how long after vaccine minimum wait before starting.

List of conditions, which are contraindications to zostivax? Options given: Unknown serostatus or history of vzv; Steroids, a high dose; Hairy cell leukemia; CGD; COPD on intermittent steroids for max 7 days, up to 20mg/d

questions.model_answer:
a) Efficacy of Zostavax in reducing shingles incidence: approximately 51% (about 50%) reduction in herpes zoster incidence overall (and about 67% reduction in postherpetic neuralgia).
b) Age: recommended for adults ≥60 years of age.
c) Anti-TNF therapy: wait a minimum of 4 weeks after the live zoster vaccine before starting anti-TNF (immunosuppressive) therapy.
d) Contraindications from the list: high-dose corticosteroids, hairy cell leukemia, and chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) are contraindications (all significantly immunocompromising states in which a live vaccine is unsafe). Unknown VZV serostatus/history is NOT a contraindication (vaccine can still be given). COPD on intermittent low/moderate-dose steroids (≤20 mg/day for ≤7 days) is NOT a contraindication (short-course, non-immunosuppressive dosing).

questions.question: Varicella vaccination

parts.text: What is the main difference in formulation between the varicella vaccine and the live shingles vaccine?
What vaccine to give in: 30F with varicella IgG negative, not pregnant
What vaccine to give in: 51M with previous chickenpox
What vaccine to give in: 68F with varicella IgG negative, not immunocompromised
List three advantages of the recombinant herpes zoster vaccine over the live attenuated vaccine.

questions.model_answer:
a) The recombinant/live shingles vaccine formulations differ in that the live attenuated zoster vaccine (Zostavax) contains a much higher titre (~14-fold) of the same Oka varicella-zoster strain than the varicella vaccine (Varivax), needed to boost the already-primed but waning cell-mediated immunity in older adults; the newer recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) instead uses a non-live VZV glycoprotein E antigen with an adjuvant.
b) 30F, varicella IgG negative, not pregnant: give the 2-dose varicella (Varivax) vaccine series.
c) 51M with prior chickenpox: no varicella vaccine needed (immune from natural infection); not yet in the standard age range for routine zoster vaccination (typically recommended starting age 50 for Shingrix), so no zoster vaccine indicated purely based on this history.
d) 68F, varicella IgG negative, not immunocompromised: give the 2-dose varicella (Varivax) vaccine series, as she is non-immune and has no contraindication to a live vaccine.
e) Advantages of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) over live attenuated (Zostavax): (1) Significantly higher efficacy against herpes zoster (>90% vs ~50%). (2) Can be safely given to immunocompromised individuals (non-live vaccine). (3) More durable, longer-lasting protection over time.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI/Canadian Immunization Guide varicella and herpes zoster vaccine chapters.

questions.question: [image-based question: Photograph of patient with herpes zoster and impetigo rash over right side of face.]

parts.text: What is this condition?
List TWO neurologic symptoms associated with this condition.

questions.model_answer:
a) Condition: Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) - reactivation of VZV in the geniculate ganglion - with secondary bacterial impetiginization of the involved skin.
b) Two neurologic symptoms: (1) ipsilateral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy (2) vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) involvement causing hearing loss, tinnitus, and/or vertigo.

questions.question: 30s pregnant female at 12 weeks gestational age who had varicella exposure 5 days ago. No previous varicella infection, not vaccinated and her VZV IgG is negative.

parts.text: What is the approximate risk of congenital varicella syndrome for this patient?
What are 2 manifestations of congenital varicella syndrome?
What is the timing of VZIG post exposure?

questions.model_answer:
a) Risk of congenital varicella syndrome: approximately 0.4-2% when maternal varicella occurs in the first 20 weeks of gestation (risk at 12 weeks is on the lower end of this range, roughly 0.4-1%).
b) Two manifestations of congenital varicella syndrome: (1) limb hypoplasia/limb defects (2) cicatricial (dermatomal scarring) skin lesions - chorioretinitis, cataracts, and microcephaly/CNS abnormalities are other manifestations.
c) Timing of VariZIG: administer as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within 96 hours (4 days); it can still be given up to 10 days post-exposure per current guidance.
questions.beyond_mandell: Precise CVS incidence figures and VariZIG's extended 10-day window reflect current AAP/CDC guidance beyond the chapter excerpt.

questions.question: Q34 (2023, PM). Pregnant woman not vaccinated or immune to varicella, 12 or 20 weeks pregnant (don't recall). Develops primary varicella infection. (PREGNANCY)

parts.text: Risk of congenital varicella in this case
2 symptoms of congenital varicella syndrome
Latest you can give VZIG

cohort_answer.text:
Risk of congenital VZV: Highest risk is <20 weeks gestation, about 1-2% of cases (Spec); 0.4-2% (ACOG).
Congenital VZV Syndrome symptoms: Dermatomal skin scarring; limb hypoplasia; ocular defects (cataracts, chorioretinitis, microphthalmia); neurologic defects (microcephaly, cortical atrophy); IUGR.
VZIG timing: For baby, indicated when lesions develop 5 days before birth to 48 hours after delivery. Generally optimally within 96 hours, up to 10 days post-exposure. (ACOG: oral acyclovir if started within 24 hours reduces duration/number of new lesions; should generally be considered for maternal infection to reduce morbidity/mortality of varicella pneumonia, but does not prevent congenital syndrome. Infants given VZIG -5 days to 2 days post delivery, and IV acyclovir if develop varicella within first 14 days of life.)

questions.question:
Q27 (2011 PM, 2008)
4 neuro complications of reactivated zoster?

parts.text: 4 neuro complications of reactivated zoster?

cohort_answer.text: Postherpetic neuralgia: pain >3 months following zoster. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve - periorbital rash, keratitis, conjunctivitis, uveitis. Ramsay Hunt Syndrome: facial and auditory nerves - ear pain, vesicles in canal, tinnitus, facial droop, ageusia. Myelopathy: post-infectious myelitis, progressive myelitis in immunocompromised hosts (fatal). Bell palsy. Stroke (BMC Infect Dis 2017): herpes zoster and herpes zoster ophthalmicus associated with increased risk. Meningitis syndromes: meningitis, meningoencephalitis, meningoradiculitis, cerebellitis.

questions.question:
Q28 (2006 PM)
A neurologist calls you about a patient with Ramsay-Hunt syndrome.

parts.text: A) What are the clinical features of Ramsay-Hunt syndrome?
B) What is the causative organism?
C) Where is the location of the neurological lesion?

cohort_answer.text:
A) VZV reactivation involving geniculate ganglion and spread to CN VIII. Classic triad: 1) ipsilateral facial paralysis, 2) ear pain, 3) vesicles in auditory canal or auricle. Other features: ipsilateral altered taste perception and tongue lesions, hearing abnormalities (decreased hearing, tinnitus, hyperacusis), lacrimation, vertigo. Decreased likelihood of recovery of facial nerve palsy.

B) VZV.

C) Geniculate ganglion of CN VII, spread to CN VIII.

No vaccine for newborn, no VZIG unless meets requirements: Premature infants >28 weeks GA exposed during hospital stay and mom not immune; Premature infants <28 weeks GA exposed during hospital stay regardless of mom's immunity; infants <1000g exposed during hospital stay regardless of mom's immunity; Newborns of moms with primary varicella 5 days before delivery up to 2 days post-partum
Determine who is susceptible or immune; Determine level of risk; For susceptible, provide vaccine (within 3 d of exposure); VZIG for immunocompromised or pregnant (within 10 d of exposure); Isolate from day 8 from first exposure to day 21 from last exposure, or to day 28 if given immunoglobulin; Immune HCW should monitored from day 8-21

questions.question: Given a scenario regarding exposure to patient who develops varicella. What (if any) clinical measures to take, including infection control and prevention for each of the following assuming exposure AND susceptible:

parts.text: A. Pregnant nurse with exposure in emergency department
B. Healthy male nurse with exposure while on ward
C. Patient with recent BMT two months ago, engrafted, prolonged exposure in clinic setting
D. What is the period of infectivity for exposed and susceptible contacts?
E. What are two important questions to ask of all exposed individuals
F. Describe management options

cohort_answer.text:
Determine if exposure meets threshold for prophylaxis; determine first possible time of contact; give VZIG (ASAP, up to 10 days acceptable), consider IVIG if VZIG unavailable, consider pre-emptive acyclovir/valacyclovir x7 days if IG not available. Exclusion from work days 8-28
Administer varicella vaccine ASAP within 3 days if no contraindications, second dose >28 days later. Exclusion from work days 8-21
Similar to pregnancy, cannot give live vaccine. Give VZIG up to 10 days after exposure, avoid other immunocompromised patients days 8-28 if VZIG given. High risk situation - consider acyclovir prophylaxis
Days 8-21 post-exposure (8-28 if VZIG given), or from days -2 until all lesions crusted over
Evidence of immunity: Have you had clinical chicken pox or been vaccinated before? Vaccine contraindications: Is there a chance you could be immunocompromised or pregnant?
Monitor; Vaccinate; IVIG; isolation considerations: symptom monitoring, isolation, prolonged post IVIG

Pre-BMT patient management
HCW in contact with ortho pt management

questions.question: Zostavax

parts.text: How much does it reduce risk of shingles and PHN?
What are the neurologic complications of Zoster?
Indications to treat zoster with IV acyclovir?

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax (live attenuated): reduces herpes zoster incidence by 51% and PHN incidence by 67% vs placebo. Shingrix (recombinant): 95% effective preventing herpes zoster, 90-100% effective reducing PHN, longer immunity. B) PHN (most common); herpes zoster ophthalmicus; CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis); Ramsay-Hunt syndrome; acute retinal necrosis; myelitis, GBS; stroke-like syndrome (cerebral angiitis). C) Any organ-threatening disease; immunocompromise; unable to tolerate PO.

questions.question: Zoster vaccine

parts.text: Differences between varicella vaccines?
Indication?
How does age modify the vaccine's effect?

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax: live attenuated vaccine. Shingrix: inactivated (recombinant glycoprotein E vaccine with AS01B adjuvant). RZV superior to ZVL in reducing herpes zoster incidence and PHN in patients >60. B) Zostavax: immunocompetent patients ≥50 without contraindications when Shingrix contraindicated/unavailable; contraindications include immunosuppression, hypersensitivity history, pregnancy, precaution in breastfeeding. Shingrix: ≥50yo without contraindications (including prior Zostavax or zoster episode), immunocompromised adults ≥50yo, post-herpes zoster ≥1 year after episode; 2 doses; contraindications hypersensitivity, precaution in pregnancy/breastfeeding/immunocompromised. C) Zostavax effectiveness declines with advanced age (delayed effectiveness); Shingrix efficacy is higher and declines more slowly with age than Zostavax.

questions.question: Congenital varicella

parts.text: A) What are the characteristic clinical findings of congenital varicella?
B) Pregnant woman early in gestation exposed to chickenpox. What is the risk to baby of VZV embryopathy and what are the clinical manifestations of VZV embryopathy?

cohort_answer.text:
IUGR; Cicatrical (scarring) skin lesions; Ocular deficits (cataracts, chorioretinitis, micro-ophthalmos, nystagmus); Limb hypoplasia; CNS (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability)
If mom immune, no concerns. If non-immune: incidence of congenital abnormalities 0.4% if maternal infection before 12th week, increases to ~2% between weeks 13-20. Rarely occurs beyond 20 weeks

questions.question: VZV exposure in pregnancy. You get a call on April 2nd about a pregnant woman whose son has just had chicken pox. He developed the rash on March 27. It has now crusted over.

parts.text: What do you do for the pregnant patient?
For how long should she be isolated?
If the woman develops varicella, how would you treat it?

cohort_answer.text: A) Determine susceptibility of host; determine infectious period (2 days before vesicle formation = March 25 until April 2, last exposure, as all vesicles have crusted over); if susceptible and within 10 day window from first exposure, give VZIG to mom. B) Start isolation today (April 2) until 28d (since given VZIG) after date of crusting of son (April 30). C) Acyclovir, start within 72h of onset of rash (better <24h). Treat chickenpox for adults with antiviral regardless of vaccine status. Peds: no treatment if <12yo and healthy; treat if >12 and unvaccinated OR chronic cutaneous/pulmonary disorders, those receiving long-term salicylate therapy, or short/intermittent corticosteroid courses.

questions.question:
Q32 (2011 PM, 2008)
Picture of side of guys face with vesicles
[image-based question: photo of a patient's face showing vesicular lesions, likely dermatomal, used to diagnose a herpes zoster-related syndrome]

parts.text: A) Diagnosis
B. 2 neuro complications
C. Also: describe herpes zoster opthalmicus and complications

cohort_answer.text:
A: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus - reactivation of VZV within the trigeminal ganglion

B: Post-herpetic neuralgia. Acute retinal necrosis. (Additional neurological complications of Ramsay Hunt: Ipsilateral facial paralysis, Ipsilateral altered taste perception and tongue lesions, Hearing abnormalities, lacrimation, vestibular disturbances (vertigo). Additional neurological complications of VZV: Post-herpetic neuralgia, Acute retinal necrosis, Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Aseptic meningitis, Encephalitis, Peripheral motor neuropathy, Myelitis, Guillain Barre syndrome, Stroke (VZV vasculopathy) - Moya moya, Cerebellitis)

C: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus - Herpes zoster involvement of the ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve. HZO begins with a prodrome of headache, malaise, and fever. Unilateral pain or hypesthesia in the affected eye, forehead, and top of the head may precede or follow the prodrome. With the onset of the rash, hyperemic conjunctivitis, uveitis, episcleritis, and keratitis may occur; ptosis is rare. Acute keratitis typically involves the epithelial, stromal, or endothelial layers of the cornea. Patients who develop epithelial or stromal keratitis are most at risk for vision loss. Vesicular lesions on the side or tip of the nose correlate highly with eye involvement (Hutchinson's sign). Early diagnosis and treatment is critical to prevent progressive corneal involvement and potential loss of vision. Zoster sine herpete - severe ear pain and facial weakness without rash, very difficult to clinically distinguish from Bell's palsy; has been reported to comprise up to 30% of Ramsay Hunt cases

questions.question: Regarding vaccines for Varicella:

parts.text: What is the main difference between Varivax and Zostavax.
31 M with no chickenpox and no immunity, immunocompetent - which vaccine?
51M with previous chickenpox, immunocompetent - which vaccine?
63F with previous shingles, immunocompetent - which vaccine?
3 reasons the currently recommended varicella vaccine is better than the previous vaccine.

cohort_answer.text: Difference: Varivax given >12 months of age; Zostavax for age >50. Scenarios: 31M no chickenpox/no immunity - Varivax; 51M with previous chickenpox - Zostavax; 63F with previous shingles - Zostavax. Reasons Shingrix (recombinant zoster) better: better immunogenicity (>90% effective vs 50%); safer; can use in immunocompromised host. Indications: age >50 who previously received Zostavax or had HZ (after at least 1 year); >18y at increased HZ risk due to immunodeficiency/immunosuppression.

questions.question: PM 11. What is the most likely infectious cause of the following congenital findings? periventricular calcifications (0.5); cutaneous scarring (0.5); heart failure (0.5); Osteitis (0.5); Cataracts (0.5)

parts.text: Identify the infectious cause for each congenital finding

questions.question: Congenital infections associated with:

parts.text: Osteitis
Periventricular calcifications
Scarring
Heart failure
Cataracts

questions.model_answer: Congenital infection associations: Osteitis - congenital syphilis (also rubella causing metaphyseal lucencies). Periventricular calcifications - congenital CMV (classically periventricular, vs toxoplasmosis which is diffuse/scattered). Scarring (cutaneous) - congenital varicella syndrome (zigzag cicatricial skin scarring). Heart failure (hydrops) - congenital parvovirus B19 (fetal anemia/hydrops) or CMV myocarditis. Cataracts - congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.question: Post BMT patient at 15 months. Exposed to room-mate with chicken pox.

parts.text: What do you do? Period of infectivity for the patient?
What are the vaccines indicated for her at 12 months assuming well and no immune suppression
When can you give VZV vaccine for her and what would be 2 contraindications at that time?

cohort_answer.text: A) Confirm diagnosis; incubation 14-16 days (range 10-21); infectivity 24-48h pre-exanthem until all lesions crusted (day 8-21 post-exposure isolation, 28 if VZIG used); confirm vaccine/infection/serologic status; VZV-seronegative HCT recipients transplanted within previous 24 months (or >24 months if continued immunosuppression e.g. chronic GVHD) should get VariZIG within 10 days of contact; seropositive but highly immunosuppressed patients should also get VariZIG; cannot give vaccine post-BMT until at least 2 years; isolate roommate in airborne; isolate BMT patient in airborne from day 8 post-exposure until day 28 (VZIG given). B) Immunize with 2 doses of Shingrix at least 1 year after herpes zoster episode; other vaccines 12 months post-BMT include 3 doses PCV at 3-6 months then PPV-23 at 12-18 months, HiB conjugate 3 doses at 6 months, Td at 6 months, inactivated polio at 6 months, HepB 3 doses at 6 months, HPV 3 doses at 6 months, meningococcal at 6 months, influenza 4-6 months post-transplant; live vaccines (MMR, varicella, YF) at 24 months post-BMT. C) Live attenuated Zostavax: wait 24 months post-transplant; inactivated Shingrix: wait 3-6 months post-transplant. Contraindications: hypersensitivity reaction; ongoing immunosuppression (for GVHD); IVIG (last 8-11 months).
